[W1981227361] (2001, economics) Measuring internal trade distances: a new method applied to estimate provincial border effects in Canada. In this paper we suggest an improved methodology for comparing the intensity of trade across and within national and provincial boundaries. Earlier efforts to assess border effects for provinces or for countries without internal trade statistics made fairly arbitrary assumptions about average distances for internal trade flows. We improve on earlier efforts by taking more complete account of the distribution of population within each province or country. Internal distance is estimated as a population-weighted average of intra-city and intercity distances as well as distances to and within rural areas. We find higher estimates of internal distances, and hence border effects, than found in previous studies.

[W2260141897] (2016, economics) International R&D Collaboration and Strategic Trade Policy. Abstract We study an international trade model with symmetric countries and symmetric firms, with countries making strategic trade policies, anticipating the decisions of firms on R&D collaboration at the subsequent stage. In general we should observe a conflict between the equilibrium outcome and the efficient one. We find that an asymmetric outcome where one country unilaterally liberalizes trade while the other does not is likely to occur. We also find that while banning international R&D collaboration may help to reach free trade equilibrium in certain situations, it provides little assistance in reaching the outcome that maximizes global welfare.

[W622286120] (2012, transport) Australian and international scan of public transport advocacy and information campaigns. Advocacy is the active support of a cause or course of action. This study investigated advocacy campaigns and initiatives that are targeted at: government and decision makers to improve public transport and the public to encourage greater public transport use. This research aims to identify public transport advocacy organisations and their most successful campaigns conducted in Australia and internationally, therefore showcasing best practice. A literature review and internet search identified public transport advocacy groups operating in Australia and internationally. From the identification of 70 organisations, a short list of the ten most effective was invited to take part in a telephone/email survey to gain a better understanding of advocacy techniques. The ten organisations interviewed included very large international organisations such as International Association of Public Transport (UiTP), to local user groups such as the Campaign for Better Transport New Zealand. The survey was structured in two parts, a quantitative component that asked respondents to name all the campaigns that they had run and a qualitative component which derived more detail on the most successful campaign as nominated by the respondent. This research found there were many different techniques used to create successful public transport advocacy campaigns including large community education campaigns, research reports submitted to government, petitions, surveys, television advertisements and sustainable transport awards. The survey enabled identification of common trends in public transport advocacy, factors in success, advocacy barriers and gaps in knowledge. This research will be useful in helping other organisations develop or improve public transport advocacy initiatives.
